Quarter-wave matching layer for a quantum potential step (k1​a=π/2,k12​=k0​k2​)

Words: 57
Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
For a constant-mass one-dimensional particle propagating through three regions of potentials 0,V1​,V0​, let kj​ be the real positive wavevectors. A layer with k1​a=π/2 makes the two interface reflection amplitudes cancel exactly when k12​=k0​k2​. Equivalently E−V1​=E(E−V0​)​. For an increasing intermediate step this requires E>V0​ and V0​/2<V1​<V0​. The result follows from r=(r01​+r12​e2ik1​a)/(1+r01​r12​e2ik1​a) and rij​=(ki​−kj​)/(ki​+kj​).

Discrete-state continuum scattering amplitude (fk​=−A/(E−ϵ+iAk))

Words: 44
Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
For a real point coupling g between a three-dimensional continuum and one discrete state, A=mg2/(2πℏ2). After the short-distance level shift is absorbed, the isotropic amplitude has the displayed form. The imaginary part is fixed by the outgoing boundary condition, and Im(1/fk​)=−k supplies elastic unitarity.

Scattering cross-section (σ=Rsc​/jin​)

Words: 90 Articles: 1
Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
A scattering cross-section divides the scattered rate per target by the incident particle flux. Its differential form resolves that rate by outgoing direction. It has units of area for three-dimensional scattering and length for two-dimensional scattering. In two dimensions, the convention ψ∼eikrcosθ+eiπ/4f(θ)eikr/kr​ gives dσ/dθ=∣f(θ)∣2/k by comparing outgoing and incident probability currents.

Scattering plane

Words: 40
Scattering cross-section OurBigBook.com
The plane spanned by incoming and outgoing propagation directions when those directions are not parallel or antiparallel. Polarization perpendicular or parallel to it is useful when expressing a differential scattering cross-section. The plane is not unique at exact forward or backward scattering.

Step potential (V(x)=V0​Θ(x))

Words: 314 Articles: 3
Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
For constant mass m, a finite jump from potential energy zero at x<0 to V0​>0 at x>0 requires continuity of the wavefunction and its first derivative. With incidence only from the left and E>V0​, put k=2mE​/ℏ and q=2m(E−V0​)​/ℏ. Matching A+B=C and k(A−B)=qC gives reflected probability amplitude B/A=(k−q)/(k+q) and transmission amplitude C/A=2k/(k+q). The transmission probability is (q/k)∣C/A∣2, conserving probability current.
For 0<E<V0​, replace q by iκ, where κ=2m(V0​−E)​/ℏ is the tunnelling decay constant. The right-hand wavefunction is Ce−κx, with zero probability current. Its probability density decays on length 1/(2κ), while its amplitude decays on length 1/κ. The semi-infinite raised region gives total reflection, unlike a finite potential barrier allowing quantum tunnelling into a second allowed region.

Evanescent amplitude versus transmitted current (j[Te−αx]=0)

Words: 60
Step potential OurBigBook.com
For a real positive decay coefficient alpha, a stationary exponential tail has zero probability current because Im(ψ∗∂x​ψ)=0. Matching a subthreshold potential step can nevertheless give a nonzero coefficient T with ∣T∣2>1 relative to a unit incident plane-wave amplitude. This measures the density just beyond the step, not a flux-transmission probability. It describes penetration without a propagating outgoing channel in the semi-infinite high-potential region.

Quantum reflection at a downward step (E→0+:r→−1, t→0, R→1, T→0)

Words: 58
Step potential OurBigBook.com
For V0​<0, k=2mE​/ℏ tends to zero as E→0+ while q=2m(E+∣V0​∣)​/ℏ stays finite. Matching gives probability amplitudes r=(k−q)/(k+q) and t=2k/(k+q), so quantum reflection probability R=r2→1 and transmission probability T=(q/k)∣t∣2∼4k/q→0. The final region is classically allowed; reflection results from the abrupt spatial change in the wavefunction's wavenumber. These are limits of positive-energy incoming states, not a flux ratio evaluated at exactly zero incident current.

Potential-step threshold wavefunction (ψ(x)=2Acos(kx) (x≤0),ψ(x)=2A (x>0))

Words: 91
Step potential OurBigBook.com
For a positive step potential and left incidence, take E→V0+​ at fixed incident probability amplitude A. The transmitted wavenumber tends to zero while the incident wavenumber tends to k=2mV0​​/ℏ. Wavefunction matching at a finite potential step gives reflected amplitude A and transmitted amplitude 2A, producing the spatial wavefunction in the title. The left probability density is 4∣A∣2cos2kx and the right density 4∣A∣2. The transmitted probability current still tends to zero because its velocity tends to zero. Over adjacent intervals of length 2π/k, the right integrated density is twice the left. These ratios use finite local integrals of a non-normalizable stationary scattering state.

Coulomb distortion in electron scattering

Words: 25
Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
The change in incident and outgoing electron wavefunctions caused by the target Coulomb potential. It can invalidate a plane wave treatment in the Born approximation, especially for a large target atomic number.

Scattering channel

Words: 40
Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
A specified asymptotic configuration of the particles and their internal quantum states in quantum scattering. An incoming channel can scatter into several outgoing channels; S-matrix elements give their probability amplitudes with a stated probability current normalization. A channel can be energetically inaccessible even when other channels are open.

Scattering angle (θ)

Words: 19
Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
The angle between specified incoming and outgoing directions in a collision; the reference frame and outgoing particle must be stated.

X-ray scattering techniques

Words: 59 Articles: 1
Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
X-ray scattering techniques use the change in a scattered photon's direction and, in inelastic measurements, its energy to probe matter. Inelastic X-ray scattering transfers energy to excitations such as phonons; elastic methods probe spatial structure without that energy transfer.

Inelastic X-ray scattering

Words: 27
X-ray scattering techniques OurBigBook.com
Inelastic X-ray scattering measures energy and momentum transferred from X-rays to matter. With sufficiently high energy resolution, it can map a phonon dispersion relation by measuring inelastic peaks at different momentum transfers. Crystal momentum is determined modulo a reciprocal lattice vector.

Inelastic scattering

Words: 18
Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
In inelastic scattering, the participants exchange energy with internal degrees of freedom, so their total translational kinetic energy need not be conserved.

Quantum reflection probability (R=∣r∣2)

Words: 171 Articles: 2
Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
For one-dimensional scattering from a real potential, write the left exterior wavefunction as eikx+re−ikx with k>0. The reflected-to-incident probability-current ratio is R=∣r∣2, since both components have the same speed and their currents have opposite signs. This probability differs from the complex reflection amplitude r. With transmission into a right exterior wavenumber q, the transmission probability is T=(q/k)∣t∣2 and conservation of current gives R+T=1 when there is no absorption.

Quantum reflection amplitude (r=Areflected​/Aincident​)

Words: 49
Quantum reflection probability OurBigBook.com
A quantum reflection amplitude is the complex ratio of the outgoing reflected wave to the incident wave in a chosen scattering convention. In one reflected channel with the same exterior speed, the reflection probability is ∣r∣2. Its phase affects interference even when its modulus is one; shifting the reference plane changes that phase.

Quantum step-reflection phase (r=(k−iκ)/(k+iκ),δ=−2arctan(κ/k))

Words: 54
Quantum reflection probability OurBigBook.com
A particle incident below a semi-infinite step has a unit-modulus quantum reflection amplitude but a nontrivial phase. Continuity of the oscillating and evanescent solutions yields the displayed coefficient, for the incident phase origin at the interface. Its decaying exterior wave has zero net probability current. The phase depends on the chosen scattering convention; the unit reflection probability does not.

Transmission amplitude (ψ∼eikL​X+re−ikL​X (X→−∞),ψ∼teikR​X (X→+∞))

Words: 58
Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
For one-dimensional quantum scattering, t is the complex amplitude of the outgoing transmitted wave relative to the incoming wave. The transmission probability is ∣t∣2 times the ratio of transmitted and incident flux velocities; with equal asymptotic dispersion it is ∣t∣2. A reflectionless potential has r=0 and a unit-modulus transmission amplitude whose phase shifts continuum quantization. The supersymmetric factorization of the one-soliton potential gives t(k)=(k+im)/(k−im) for its single-bound-state potential.

S-matrix (S)

Words: 411 Articles: 7
Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
The S-matrix maps incoming asymptotic states to outgoing asymptotic states. Its connected transition matrix elements contain an overall energy-momentum Dirac delta function and an invariant scattering amplitude. In quantum field theory, the LSZ reduction formula obtains these elements from amputated field correlators.

Redundant pole of a scattering matrix

Words: 61
S-matrix OurBigBook.com
A pole of a scattering matrix arising from the numerator F(−k) rather than a zero of the incoming Jost function F(k) can fail to correspond to a bound state. For F(k)=(k−iκ)/(k+iα), the pole at iκ is associated with the incoming zero; the pole at iα comes from the numerator. The regular Eckart realization has α>κ. The distinction and this explicit example are discussed in dipot.ulb.ac.be/dspace/bitstream/2013/373712/4/2306.12216.pdf.

Jost function (F(k))

Words: 49
S-matrix OurBigBook.com
For radial quantum scattering, the incoming coefficient of the regular solution defines the Jost function, with convention S(k)=F(−k)/F(k). A zero at k=iκ, κ>0, removes the exponentially growing component and produces a bound state, subject to regularity and normalizability. Poles of the outgoing numerator alone need not produce bound states.

Unit-modulus hyperbolic scattering block (Su​(θ)=sinh[(θ+iu)/2]/sinh[(θ−iu)/2])

Words: 76
S-matrix OurBigBook.com
For real u, this scalar S-matrix block satisfies Su​(θ)Su​(−θ)=1 and Hermitian analyticity of a two-particle S-matrix. It therefore has modulus one for real rapidity differences. For 0<u<π its pole at θ=iu has residue 2isinu and admits a direct-channel bound-state pole interpretation. Its crossed block is cosh[(θ−iu)/2]/cosh[(θ+iu)/2]. The endpoints u=0 and u=π are removable degeneracies giving constant amplitudes, so a particle cannot be inferred there from the uncancelled denominator alone. This block specifies an amplitude; a complete theory must also obey the remaining crossing symmetry and bootstrap fusion constraints.

Physical rapidity strip (0<Imϑ<π)

Words: 156 Articles: 2
S-matrix OurBigBook.com
For relativistic two-body scattering in one spatial dimension, this strip is the standard domain containing bound-state and crossed-channel poles. A stable-particle interpretation requires appropriate pole kinematics and residues; not every singularity automatically represents a new particle. Crossing relates rapidity ϑ to iπ−ϑ.

Crossed-channel pole in diagonal factorized scattering (t(iα)=ma2​+mb2​−2ma​mb​cosα)

Words: 75
Physical rapidity strip OurBigBook.com
A physical-strip pole of a diagonal S-matrix can come from exchange of an existing particle in the crossed channel. For external masses ma​,mb​, use the momentum difference, rather than the sum, to identify the exchanged mass through the displayed invariant. Crossing symmetry turns the pole at iα into a direct pole at i(π−α) of the particle-antiparticle channel. For mB​=2mcos(u/2), the pole of SBA​ at iu/2 has t=m2 and exchanges the existing charge-one particle; it is not a new charge-three bound state.

Relativistic bound-state mass from a rapidity pole (mc2​=ma2​+mb2​+2ma​mb​cosu)

Words: 40
Physical rapidity strip OurBigBook.com
At relative rapidity iu, the analytically continued sum of the constituent four-momentum vectors is on the bound-state mass shell with the displayed mass. For equal constituents, rapidities χ±iu/2 sum to 2ma​cos(u/2)(coshχ,sinhχ). A pole at u=0 is at threshold rather than a strictly bound state.

Hermitian analyticity of a two-particle S-matrix

Words: 37
S-matrix OurBigBook.com
In a real species basis, the two-particle S-matrix satisfies S(−θ∗)=S(θ)† under the usual scattering analyticity assumptions. On the real rapidity axis this relates inverse-rapidity amplitudes to complex conjugates. Combined with the algebraic inverse relation S(θ)S(−θ)=I, it gives physical unitarity.

For a localized target and a plane wave incident along the z-axis, the large-radius scattering wavefunction has the form
ψ(r)∼eikz+f(θ,ϕ)reikr​,

Scattering state

Words: 17
Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
A scattering state is a state used to describe quantum scattering. Its asymptotic incoming and outgoing components determine a scattering amplitude.

Partial wave

Words: 54 Articles: 1
Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
A partial wave is a component of a scattering state with definite orbital angular momentum. A central potential preserves each angular-momentum channel, so the scattering problem decomposes into independent partial waves.

D wave (ℓ=2)

Words: 27
Partial wave OurBigBook.com
A partial wave with orbital angular momentum ℓ=2. Its orbital parity is positive. Coupling it to a spin-one pair can include total J=1, allowing a D wave component in the deuteron.

Partial-wave scattering

Words: 96 Articles: 1
Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
Partial-wave scattering decomposes a scattering state into partial waves with definite orbital angular momentum. For a central potential, each channel has its own scattering phase shift and Partial-wave S-matrix.

Two-dimensional partial-wave scattering formula (f(θ)=2/π​∑m≥0​wm​eiδm​sinδm​cos(mθ), σ=(4/k)∑m≥0​wm​sin2δm​)

Words: 80
Partial-wave scattering OurBigBook.com
For a real central potential and the outgoing convention eiπ/4f(θ)eikr/kr​, the Partial-wave S-matrix is Sm​=e2iδm​. The cosine form of the Jacobi-Anger expansion fixes w0​=1 and wm​=2 for m≥1. Comparing the outgoing part of each phase-shifted radial cosine with the incident plane wave gives the displayed scattering amplitude. Integrating ∣f∣2/k gives the displayed scattering cross-section, since the constant angular mode has squared norm 2π and each positive-order cosine has squared norm π. Reversing the multiplicities would already fail to reproduce the free plane wave at zero scattering phase shift.

The differential scattering cross-section is the effective incident area scattered per unit solid angle. It is defined by the ratio of the outgoing particle rate through dΩ to the incident flux.

Reflected wave

Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
A reflected wave is an outgoing component travelling back toward the side from which the incident wave arrived.

Transmission probability

Words: 25
Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
The transmission probability is the ratio of transmitted to incident probability current. When the asymptotic wavenumbers agree, it is the squared modulus of the transmission amplitude.

One-dimensional S-matrix

Words: 89 Articles: 2
Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
For a reflection-invariant localized potential, order incoming amplitudes from the left and right and outgoing amplitudes toward the left and right. Then
S=(rt​tr​),
(5)
where r and t are the reflection and transmission amplitudes. Probability-current conservation makes S unitary for a real potential.

Parity basis of a one-dimensional S-matrix

Words: 29
One-dimensional S-matrix OurBigBook.com
For a parity-symmetric one-dimensional potential, the even and odd parity states diagonalize the One-dimensional S-matrix:
S+−​=S−+​=0,S=diag(S++​,S−−​).
(6)
For a real potential, unitarity further gives ∣S++​∣=∣S−−​∣=1 at real positive energy.

Quantum scattering OurBigBook.com
For a central potential, each angular-momentum channel has a scalar scattering coefficient Sl​(k)=e2iδl​(k).
Each channel coefficient is a component of the scattering matrix in a basis adapted to rotational symmetry.

Scattering phase shift (δl​)

Words: 176 Articles: 2
Partial-wave S-matrix OurBigBook.com
For elastic scattering by a real central potential, the phase shift δl​(k) measures the phase difference between the asymptotic radial wave in angular-momentum channel l and the corresponding free wave. Its channel Partial-wave S-matrix is Sl​=e2iδl​.
The phase shift parametrizes elastic partial-wave scattering, rather than general scattering phenomena.

Finite-range partial-wave threshold law (δℓ​(k)=O(k2ℓ+1))

Words: 84
Scattering phase shift OurBigBook.com
For regular low-energy elastic scattering by a finite-range central potential, higher partial waves are suppressed by their centrifugal barriers. Matching the regular interior radial solution to small-argument exterior spherical Bessel functions gives the displayed scaling of scattering phase shift, in the generic absence of a threshold singularity. Since the channel amplitude is proportional to sinδℓ​/k, it scales as k2ℓ. The ℓ=0 term is isotropic and normally leads. A tuned vanishing leading amplitude or a threshold resonance requires examining the next terms rather than applying the generic statement blindly.

Periodic-box phase-shift quantization (kn​L+δ(kn​)=2πn)

Words: 46
Scattering phase shift OurBigBook.com
For a reflectionless scattering wavefunction whose two asymptotic phases differ by δ(k), a large periodic box gives kn​L+δ(kn​)=2πn. Compared with the free value kn(0)​=2πn/L, kn​−kn(0)​=−δ(kn(0)​)/L+O(L−2) away from thresholds. Discrete bound states and phase-branch changes alter mode indexing and must be counted when comparing complete spectra.

S wave (quantum scattering, l=0)

Words: 110 Articles: 1
Partial-wave S-matrix OurBigBook.com
An S wave is the rotationally invariant angular-momentum channel l=0. At sufficiently low energy it normally dominates short-range scattering because higher partial waves are suppressed by their centrifugal barriers.

Phase shift of a delta-shell potential (tanδ0​=−kR+gsin(kR)cos(kR)gsin2(kR)​)

Words: 80
S wave (quantum scattering) OurBigBook.com
For V(r)=V0​δ(r−R), put g=2mV0​R/ℏ2. The regular reduced radial wave function is proportional to sinkr inside the shell and to sin(kr+δ0​) outside. It is continuous at R, while its radial derivative jumps by (g/R)u(R). Dividing the jump condition by the common value gives kcot(kR+δ0​)−kcot(kR)=g/R, which implies the displayed phase shift modulo π. At nodes, the undivided matching equations give the continuous limiting interpretation. For g=0, an equivalent formula is kcotδ0​=−kcot(kR)−k(kR)/[gsin2(kR)]. The exact S-wave scattering amplitude is [kcotδ0​−ik]−1.

Partial-wave expansion of a scattering amplitude

Words: 39 Articles: 1

The angle between incoming and outgoing propagation directions is χ=2θB​ for that reflection geometry. In normal-incidence backscattering, a detector's angle ϕ from the outward surface normal instead gives χ=π−ϕ; neither detector colatitude nor angle to the surface normal should silently replace θB​. Davisson–Germer experiment
Words: 360
Electron diffraction OurBigBook.com
The Davisson–Germer experiment turned elastic scattering from nickel into evidence for a matter wave. The search became a deliberate wave test in 1926, with diffraction beams found early in 1927. The earlier crystal investigation had begun in 1925; the de Broglie wavelength proposal was already present in the 1924 thesis.[ref]
A heated tungsten ribbon supplied electrons; gun apertures selected a narrow beam. Two 1mm apertures were 8mm apart; the gun ended 7mm from a nickel crystal cut parallel to its {111} planes. An adjustable electric potential difference set the speed. The beam struck normally inside an evacuated, field-free enclosure with target and outer electrodes at one potential. A double-box collector, 11mm from the target with a 1mm entrance, selected directions. A retarding electric potential difference rejected slower electrons; the inner collector fed a sensitive galvanometer. Moving the collector scanned colatitude; rotating the crystal scanned azimuth.[ref]
The readout was collected electric current, not a photograph of electron paths. Voltage scans held the gun-plate current constant because incident-beam current could not be held constant; the overall current trend therefore needed caution. A strong feature developed at 54V near 50∘ colatitude. Surface heating distinguished crystal beams from adsorbed-gas beams; finite apertures and background shifted or broadened apparent peaks.[ref]
At the bright beam's colatitude, an azimuth scan revealed three companion directions, matching crystal symmetry. The test compared wavelengths inferred from diffraction angles and known crystal spacings with wavelengths inferred from accelerating voltage and momentum; the 1937 lecture displayed this comparison against U−1/2. Agreement across beam directions supplied more evidence than one angular peak.[ref]
The inference is about coherent quantum phases in scattering probabilities. It does not establish a wavy particle trajectory, and a collector-current experiment does not resolve individual detection events. Predicting the full intensity additionally requires the material's scattering amplitude, its surface condition, and instrumental angular acceptance; the de Broglie wavelength alone predicts none of those strengths. The following finite-row electron diffraction model isolates phase addition without attempting to reproduce the nickel measurements.

Retain only one scattering event per amplitude, as in the Born approximation. For angle ϕ from the outward normal, write the adjacent-site quantum phase difference as δ=kdsinϕ, with k=2π/λ; reversing its overall sign leaves the intensity unchanged. Summing a geometric series gives
I(0)I(ϕ)​=N21​​∑j=0N−1​eijδ​2=[Nsin(δ/2)sin(Nδ/2)​]2,δ=λ2πd​sinϕ.
(14)
At δ=2πm use the continuous limit I/I(0)=1, rather than treating 0/0 as a missing peak. The integer m is the diffraction order: dsinϕ=mλ. This is a surface-row spacing, not the plane spacing in Bragg's law. The plotted intensity is normalized to its central value; it is not an integrated detection probability or an absolute collector electric current.
At 100V, λ≃0.12264nm and the positive first-order angle is arcsin(λ/d)≃29.4∘. At 400V, the wavelength halves and this angle becomes about 14.2∘. Increasing N narrows each peak through more selective interference, while increasing momentum brings a fixed-order peak nearer the normal. Unequal site amplitudes, multiple scattering, a three-dimensional crystal lattice structure factor, and finite detector acceptance can change this simple picture; it is an explanatory model with hypothetical inputs.

A tetragonal conventional cell with lattice points at its vertices and face centers describes a Bravais lattice. The reciprocal lattice of a body-centered tetragonal lattice with conventional sides a,a,b consists of 2π(h/a,k/a,l/b) with h+k+l even; these points form a face-centered tetragonal conventional cell with sides 4π/a,4π/a,4π/b.

Reciprocal lattice OurBigBook.com
A reciprocal lattice vector G has the displayed property for every direct lattice vector R. Thus eiG⋅R=1. Fourier components of a lattice-periodic potential carry these wavevectors and couple plane-wave electronic states whose momenta differ by ℏG. This is the origin of the Bragg-plane mixing in a nearly-free electron model.

Reciprocal lattice change in a structural phase transition
Words: 118
Reciprocal lattice OurBigBook.com
The reciprocal lattice of a body-centered cubic lattice is face-centred cubic, and that of a face-centered cubic lattice is body-centred cubic. In both cases its conventional cubic side is 4π/a if the direct conventional side is a. Thus a direct BCC-to-FCC phase transition reverses the reciprocal lattice types. The reciprocal primitive cell volume is (2π)3/Ω, so thermal expansion contracts reciprocal spacings, while a discontinuous change in direct primitive unit cell volume gives an inverse change in reciprocal cell volume.
A first-order structural transition need not continuously deform one perfect reciprocal array into another. Phase coexistence, new orientation variants, domains and loss of single-crystal alignment can produce two sets of diffraction peaks or many differently oriented sets. The two endpoint lattice types alone do not specify the transformation path or orientation relationship.

Crystal scattering OurBigBook.com

2k⋅q=∣q∣2,∣q∣=2ksin2θ​.

The smallest nonzero diffraction angle is determined by the shortest reciprocal-lattice vector.
This reciprocal-lattice condition is equivalent to Bragg's law, expressed in terms of the lattice-plane spacing and the wavelength.
Bragg's law (nλ=2dsinθ)
Words: 1k Articles: 4
Elastic Bragg scattering condition OurBigBook.com
Bragg's law selects directions of constructive interference in coherent elastic scattering from equally spaced lattice planes:
nλ=2dsinθ,n=1,2,3,….
(25)
Here d>0 is the perpendicular interplanar spacing, λ>0 the incident wavelength, n the positive integer diffraction order, and θ the Bragg angle, measured between the incoming beam and the lattice planes. The scattering deflection, between incoming and outgoing propagation directions, is 2θ. Thus a plotted detector angle 2θ must be halved before insertion into Bragg's law. The θ in the parent elastic Bragg scattering condition denotes the full deflection; the present θ denotes half of it. [ref]
The lattice planes organize wave interference throughout a crystal structure; they are not literal metal mirrors or separate reflecting surfaces. The picture assumes elastic scattering, hence an unchanged wavelength, and sufficiently stable relative wave phases across the contributing lattice planes. X-ray wavelengths comparable with atomic interplanar spacings make these directions experimentally accessible. The sine cannot exceed one: an order exists geometrically only if nλ/(2d)≤1. For λ>2d, even the first diffraction order is inaccessible. A geometrically possible direction need not have nonzero wave intensity; the crystal lattice structure factor and crystal basis structure factor also matter. [ref]
Bragg angle (θ)
Words: 140
Bragg's law OurBigBook.com
The Bragg angle is the glancing angle from the incident beam to the selected lattice planes, with 0<θ≤90∘. If α is instead the angle from the beam to the plane normal, α=90∘−θ and Bragg's law becomes nλ=2dcosα. Defining the angle explicitly prevents a sine-versus-cosine error as well as a factor-of-two error in the detector deflection.
Choose λ=0.154nm and d=0.200nm as an illustrative model, not historical measurements. For the first diffraction order,
sinθ=2(0.200)0.154​=0.385,θ≃22.643740∘,2θ≃45.287481∘.
(26)
The second diffraction order has sinθ=0.770 and 2θ≃100.707778∘; the third would require sinθ=1.155 and is impossible. These are different diffraction orders of the same interplanar spacing at the same wavelength.
Conversely, a first-order reflection at a measured deflection 2θ gives the interplanar spacing
d=2sinθλ​.
(27)
Using 2θ≃45.287481∘ recovers d≃0.200nm. This is the useful reversal: a known wavelength turns an angular measurement into an atomic length. An unassigned diffraction order or an unknown wavelength prevents that single measurement from determining d uniquely.
Bragg path difference (Δℓ=2dsinθ)
Words: 197
Bragg's law OurBigBook.com
Compare two rays scattered into parallel outgoing directions from neighboring lattice planes. In the diagram, A lies on the upper plane and B on the lower plane, directly beneath A with AB=d. Draw through A the incoming and outgoing equal-wave phase fronts, perpendicular to their respective rays. They meet the lower ray at C and D. Each right triangle gives CB=BD=dsinθ, so the lower ray travels the extra distance
Δℓ=CB+BD=2dsinθ.
(28)
The resulting phase difference is Δφ=2πΔℓ/λ. Constructive interference requires Δφ=2πn, which proves Bragg's law in this ray construction. Comparing equal-wave phase fronts, rather than arbitrary ray endpoints, is what makes the distance comparison meaningful.
The same geometry connects to the reciprocal lattice. With wavenumber k=2π/λ, the elastic Bragg scattering condition gives a transfer magnitude ∣q∣=2ksinθ. A reciprocal vector normal to these lattice planes has ∣q∣=2πn/d. Equating them again yields Bragg's law. The ray and reciprocal lattice descriptions therefore express the same wave phase matching.
Primitive cubic Bragg peak positions (dhkl​=a/h2+k2+l2​)

Bragg's law OurBigBook.com
Consider a chosen primitive cubic lattice aZ3 with a=0.400nm and one identical point scatterer per primitive unit cell. Retain the incident wavelength λ=0.154nm. This is an ideal point model. Its reciprocal lattice vectors are q=(2π/a)(h,k,l) for integer triples other than (0,0,0). Write S=h2+k2+l2. The associated interplanar spacing and first-order Bragg angle satisfy
dhkl​=∣q∣2π​=S​a​,sin2θ=4a2λ2​S=0.03705625S.
(29)
The reflection labels (hkl) use the Miller index convention, keeping unreduced triples to encode diffraction order. With that convention, set n=1 in Bragg's law for each label. The (200) reflection is equivalently the second diffraction order of (100): d200​=a/2 does not imply extra scatterers halfway between the occupied (100) planes. Counting both descriptions as distinct reflections would count the same direction twice.
For (100), (110), (111) and (200), respectively, S=1,2,3,4 and the calculated interplanar spacings are 0.400000, 0.282843, 0.230940 and 0.200000nm. Their calculated deflections 2θ are 22.197435∘, 31.594744∘, 38.952948∘ and 45.287481∘. Equal steps in S give equal steps in sin2θ, not equal steps in 2θ. This regularity makes an angular pattern a test of a proposed crystal structure.
A real crystal structure has a Bravais lattice together with an atomic basis of a crystal. The crystal lattice structure factor selects the periodic directions; the crystal basis structure factor combines the scattering amplitudes of atoms within a unit cell and can cancel a reflection. Consequently Bragg's law alone predicts neither allowed reflections nor their wave intensities. [ref] Systematic absences further restrict observed families; for example, face-centered cubic lattice centering permits only indices all even or all odd in conventional cubic indexing. The four strips above apply to the stated primitive cubic lattice, not to sodium chloride or a face-centered cubic lattice. [ref]
Bragg crystal reflection experiment of 1913
Words: 192
Bragg's law OurBigBook.com
William Lawrence Bragg introduced the plane interpretation; his father William Henry Bragg built the X-ray spectrometer. Their joint 1913 paper, The Reflection of X-rays by Crystals, reports the experiment. [ref] [ref]
An X-ray tube supplied radiation through lead slits to a crystal mounted with its cleavage face through the rotation axis. A rotating ionization chamber replaced a spectrometer telescope; electric current measured the scattered signal, and a circular scale supplied angular readings. They first scanned the chamber at fixed crystal orientation, then swept crystal and chamber together to follow the reflection. [ref]
Changing chamber gas checked detector dependence; readings on opposite sides checked face-setting errors. Repeated peaks with sines of half-deflections in integer ratios, together with matching absorption coefficients, distinguished repeated diffraction orders of the same wavelength from different radiation components. Comparing crystal faces constrained interplanar spacings. Their limits included slit broadening, face alignment and incomplete interception at glancing incidence; assigning absolute wavelengths still required a structural choice for d. [ref]

Systematic absence OurBigBook.com
The identical two-atom motif adds a factor 1+exp[iπ(h+k+l)/2] to the FCC lattice structure factor. Among even-index FCC diffraction reflections, only those with h+k+l divisible by4 survive. The allowed FCC reflection200 therefore vanishes for equal motif scattering amplitudes.

X-ray diffraction

Words: 1k Articles: 12
Crystal scattering OurBigBook.com
X-ray diffraction is the angular redistribution of X-ray wave intensity through wave interference between scattered waves. In a crystal structure, repeated lattice translations select discrete outgoing directions by the Laue equations. A photographic plate can therefore turn invisible atomic periodicity into a visible constellation of spots. Their geometry constrains the Bravais lattice and its orientation; their wave intensities also depend on the crystal basis structure factor. Determining atomic positions belongs to X-ray crystallography and requires more information than recognizing a spot pattern.
The Laue X-ray diffraction experiment of 1912 established this phenomenon experimentally. The Laue method uses a fixed crystal structure with a range of incident wavelengths; the Bragg crystal reflection experiment of 1913 instead measured angularly resolved signals with a moving detector. These are different ways of finding the same coherent elastic scattering directions.

Powder X-ray diffraction
Words: 107 Articles: 1
X-ray diffraction OurBigBook.com
Powder X-ray diffraction measures X-ray diffraction from many crystal grains with different orientations. For each allowed set of lattice spacings, suitable grains satisfy Bragg's law and produce a cone of diffracted directions, seen as a ring on an area detector or a peak in an angular scan. Several peak positions and systematic absences can identify a crystal structure even when a sample no longer retains one single-crystal orientation. Preferred orientation, strain and phase coexistence can complicate interpretation.

Laue equations (ai​⋅(sout​−sin​)=mi​λ)
Words: 248
X-ray diffraction OurBigBook.com
For incident and outgoing unit propagation vectors sin​ and sout​, wavelength λ>0, and primitive lattice translation vectors a1​,a2​,a3​, the Laue equations are
a1​⋅(sout​−sin​)=hλ,a2​⋅(sout​−sin​)=kλ,a3​⋅(sout​−sin​)=lλ,(h,k,l)∈Z3.
(30)
All three must hold for the same wavelength and outgoing direction. The integers label a reciprocal lattice vector; they need not be coprime. For wavevectors kin,out​=(2π/λ)sin,out​, equivalently
G=kout​−kin​=hb1​+kb2​+lb3​,ai​⋅bj​=2πδij​.
(31)
This uses angular wavenumbers; the crystallographic convention without 2π instead uses s/λ.[ref]
For a short proof, translate a scatterer through ai​. Its incident wave phase changes by kin​⋅ai​ and propagation to the same distant observation direction contributes −kout​⋅ai​. The relative wave phase factor is therefore exp(−iG⋅ai​). It equals one for all lattice translations exactly when G belongs to the reciprocal lattice. A finite crystal lattice structure factor broadens the ideal maxima; the crystal basis structure factor can cancel them. Geometric phase matching is necessary for a sharp reflection, but does not guarantee a visible spot.
For elastic scattering, the additional constraint is
∣kin​+G∣2=∣kin​∣2,2kin​⋅G+∣G∣2=0.
(32)
It is an Ewald sphere centered at −kin​ in the space of transfer vectors G. The parent elastic Bragg scattering condition uses q=kin​−kout​=−G, so its displayed condition has the opposite sign. Both give Bragg's law for the same lattice planes.
Laue method
Words: 506 Articles: 1
X-ray diffraction OurBigBook.com
In the Laue method, a fixed single crystal structure receives a collimated beam containing many wavelengths. Each reciprocal lattice vector can select its own wavelength; waves with different wavelengths need not interfere with one another. For G=0, the elastic scattering constraint gives the particularly useful test
λG​=−∣G∣24πsin​⋅G​.
(33)
A candidate reflection requires λG​>0 within the source spectrum and an outgoing ray that reaches the detector. Varying wavelength changes the radius and center of the Ewald sphere while leaving the reciprocal lattice fixed. A monochromatic wave instead fixes the radius: rotating the crystal structure or varying the incident wavelength in a scan finds reflections sequentially. A white-beam photograph integrates many spectral selections in one exposure; it is not an angular scan at one known wavelength.
The Laue method is useful for orienting a single crystal structure: tilting it changes which reciprocal lattice vectors meet the spectral and detector conditions. Absolute scale has an ambiguity if the wavelengths are unknown. Scaling all direct lattice translations by c>0 and all selected wavelengths by c leaves every outgoing direction unchanged. Independently known spectral information or length calibration is needed to remove this ambiguity.
Calculated transmission Laue pattern (λ=2am/(h2+k2+m2))
Words: 287
Laue method OurBigBook.com
Choose a primitive cubic lattice with a=0.400nm, one identical point scatterer per primitive unit cell, incident direction sin​=(0,0,1), and the continuous wavelength band 0.080≤λ≤0.160nm. This is a hypothetical model, not the zinc blende specimen of the Laue X-ray diffraction experiment of 1912. Write a candidate reciprocal lattice vector as G=(2π/a)(h,k,−m) with m>0, and set S=h2+k2+m2. The Laue equations and elastic scattering give
λ=S2am​,sout​=(S2mh​,S2mk​,1−S2m2​).
(34)
A transmission photographic plate at z=L>0 intercepts only sout,z​>0. Its coordinates relative to the direct beam are
X=Lsout,z​sout,x​​=h2+k2−m22Lmh​,Y=h2+k2−m22Lmk​.
(35)
For (h,k,−m)=(2,1,−1) and L=50mm, S=6, λ=0.13333…nm and sout​=(2/3,1/3,2/3), so (X,Y)=(50,25)mm. Its length is one, and each component difference satisfies the corresponding Laue equations. This verifies a direction and a selected wavelength, without predicting an exposure or measured wave intensity.
The first panel has fourfold symmetry because its chosen Bravais lattice, beam axis and square detector share that symmetry. For the tilted panel, apply a rotation matrix R to each index vector, set v=R(h,k,l), and use λ=−2avz​/∣v∣2 and sout​=(0,0,1)+(λ/a)v. All indices with ∣(h,k,l)∣≤2a/λmin​=10 suffice: elastic scattering bounds ∣G∣≤2∣kin​∣. Thus the plotted spectral and angular selection is complete within this ideal point model and detector window. Multiples of an index vector select inversely scaled wavelengths and can land on the same spot; a white-beam spot need not identify a unique diffraction order.
Laue X-ray diffraction experiment of 1912
Words: 158
X-ray diffraction OurBigBook.com
Max von Laue proposed crystal X-ray diffraction and wrote the theoretical section; Walther Friedrich and Paul Knipping performed the experiments.[ref]
An X-ray tube, lead apertures and shielding supplied a narrow beam through a crystal on a goniometer. Photographic plates recorded the direct beam and separate spots. Copper(II) sulfate trials preceded oriented zinc blende. Optical alignment was checked with X-rays. Removing the crystal removed the extra spots; grinding destroyed their ordered arrangement; translation preserved it, while tilt changed it. Rotation about the beam rotated the pattern.[ref]
Spots and orientation dependence supported wave interference and three-dimensional crystal periodicity. They determined neither all atomic positions nor an absolute wavelength scale. The authors left open whether the selected radiation originated as crystal fluorescence or was already in the incident beam. This differs from the modern Laue method.[ref]
The 1914 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Max von Laue; the discovery's experimental account remains jointly credited to Walther Friedrich and Paul Knipping.[ref] The subsequent inference of particular crystal structures is developed under X-ray crystallography.
